title: Security Fundamentals
description: Understand Git's security model: signing, verification, SSH, HTTPS, and token-based authentication.

data.text: Git security covers three areas: authentication (proving your identity to the remote), signing (cryptographically verifying that commits and tags come from you), and transport security (encrypting data in transit). Understanding each area protects your code and your contributors.

Git supports HTTPS and SSH for authenticating to remote repositories. HTTPS uses username/password or personal access tokens. SSH uses public/private key pairs. SSH is generally preferred for automation and personal use; HTTPS is required when firewalls block SSH.

rows: Firewall-friendly, CI systems, GitHub web UI

data.text: Both HTTPS and SSH encrypt data in transit. HTTPS uses TLS. SSH uses the SSH protocol's built-in encryption. Never use the deprecated git:// protocol, which transmits data in plaintext.

data.title: Verify transport security
data.code:
# Check remote URL protocol
git remote -v

# Secure (HTTPS):
# origin  https://github.com/example/project.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/example/project.git (push)

# Secure (SSH):
# origin  git@github.com:example/project.git (fetch)
# origin  git@github.com:example/project.git (push)

# Insecure (git://) — DO NOT USE:
# origin  git://github.com/example/project.git (fetch)

# Convert git:// to HTTPS
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/example/project.git

data.text: Git can sign commits and tags with GPG or SSH keys. A signed commit proves that the commit was created by someone who possesses the private key. This prevents impersonation and ensures the integrity of the commit content.

data.title: Configure commit signing
data.code:
# Sign commits with GPG
git config --global user.signingkey <gpg-key-id>
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

# Sign commits with SSH (Git 2.34+)
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

# Sign a single commit without changing config
git commit -S -m "chore: secure configuration"

# Verify a signed commit
git log --show-signature -1 HEAD

data.text: GitHub displays verified signatures on commits and tags. To enable this, add your public GPG or SSH key to your GitHub account. GitHub then verifies signatures against the keys you have registered.

data.title: Add a GPG key to GitHub
data.code:
# Export your GPG public key
gpg --armor --export <gpg-key-id>

# Copy the output and add it to:
# GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New GPG key

# After adding, GitHub shows 'Verified' on signed commits

# For SSH signing keys:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Add to:
# GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key

data.title: Use SSH signing where possible
data.text: SSH signing is simpler than GPG: no key generation or management overhead, and SSH keys are likely already configured for Git. GPG is useful when you need to sign emails or documents in addition to Git objects.

items.question: Does Git LFS encrypt transferred files?
items.answer: Yes. Git LFS uses HTTPS or SSH for transfer, so files are encrypted in transit. The LFS server stores files; configure server-side encryption at rest if required.

items.question: Can I sign merges?
items.answer: git merge does not create a signed commit by default. Use git merge -S to sign the merge commit, or configure commit.gpgsign to sign all commits including merges.

items.question: How do I verify a signed tag?
items.answer: Use git tag -v <tag-name> to verify a GPG-signed tag. Use git verify-tag <tag-name> for SSH-signed tags.

items.question: Can I require signed commits in a repository?
items.answer: Yes. Use a server-side hook (e.g., pre-receive hook on GitLab/GitHub Enterprise) to reject unsigned commits. GitHub does not enforce this by default for public repositories.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use HTTPS or SSH for transport security; never use git://
Git LFS encrypts files in transit via HTTPS or SSH
Sign commits with GPG or SSH to verify authorship
Add your public key to GitHub to enable verified signatures
SSH signing is simpler than GPG for Git-only use cases
